items.body: Cecil Taylor26 languagesFrom Wikipedia, the free encyclopediaFor the Scottish playwright, see C. P. Taylor.Cecil TaylorTaylor at Moers Festival 2008Background informationBornCecil Percival TaylorMarch 25, 1929Long Island City, New York, U.S.DiedApril 5, 2018 (aged 89)Brooklyn, New York, U.S.GenresJazz, avant-garde jazz, free jazz, free improvisationOccupationsMusician, bandleader, composer, improviser, poetInstrumentPianoYears active1956–2018LabelsTransition, Blue Note, Freedom, Hathut, Enja, FMPCecil Percival Taylor (March 25, 1929 – April 5, 2018)[1][2][3] was an American pianist and poet.[4][5]Taylor was classically trained and was one of the pioneers of free jazz. His music is characterized by an energetic, physical approach, resulting in complex improvisation often involving tone clusters and intricate polyrhythms. His technique has been compared to percussion. Referring to the number of keys on a standard piano, Val Wilmer used the phrase "eighty-eight tuned drums" to describe Taylor's style.[6] He has been referred to as "Art Tatum with contemporary-classical leanings".[7]Early life and educationeditCecil Percival Taylor was born on March 25, 1929, in Long Island City, Queens,[8] and raised in Corona, Queens.[9] As an only child in a middle-class family, Taylor was encouraged by his mother, Almeda Ragland Taylor, to play music at an early age. He began playing piano at age six and went on to study at the New York College of Music and New England Conservatory in Boston. At the New England Conservatory, Taylor majored in popular music arrangement. During his time there, he also became familiar with contemporary European art music. Bela Bartók and Karlheinz Stockhausen notably influenced his music.[10]In 1955, Taylor moved back to New York City from Boston. He formed a quartet with soprano saxophonist Steve Lacy, bassist Buell Neidlinger, and drummer Dennis Charles.[10] Taylor's first recording, Jazz Advance, featured Lacy and was released in 1956.[11] The recording is described by Richard Cook and Brian Morton in the Penguin Guide to Jazz: "While there are still many nods to conventional post-bop form in this set, it already points to the freedoms in which the pianist would later immerse himself."[12] Taylor's quartet featuring Lacy also appeared at the 1957 Newport Jazz Festival, which was made into the album At Newport.[13] Taylor collaborated with saxophonist John Coltrane in 1958 on Stereo Drive, now available as Coltrane Time.[14]1950s and early 1960seditThroughout the 1950s and 1960s, Taylor's music grew more complex and moved away from existing jazz styles. Gigs were often hard to come by, and club owners found that Taylor's approach of playing long pieces tended to impede business.[15] His 1959 LP record Looking Ahead! showcased his innovation as a creator as compared to the jazz mainstream. Unlike others at the time, Taylor utilized virtuosic techniques and made swift stylistic shifts from phrase to phrase. These qualities, among others, still remained notable distinctions of his music for the rest of his life.[16]Landmark recordings, such as Unit Structures (1966), also appeared. Within the Cecil Taylor Unit (a distinction that was often used at performances and recordings between 1962 and 2006 for a shifting group of sidemen), musicians were able to develop new forms of conversational interplay. In the early 1960s, an uncredited Albert Ayler worked with Taylor, jamming and appearing on at least one recording, Four, which was unreleased until appearing on the 2004 Ayler box set Holy Ghost: Rare & Unissued Recordings (1962–70).[17]By 1961, Taylor was working regularly with alto saxophonist Jimmy Lyons, who would become one of his most important and consistent collaborators. Taylor, Lyons, and drummer Sunny Murray (and later Andrew Cyrille) formed the core personnel of the Cecil Taylor Unit, Taylor's primary ensemble until Lyons' death in 1986. Lyons' playing, strongly influenced by jazz icon Charlie Parker, retained a strong blues sensibility and helped keep Taylor's increasingly avant garde music tethered to the jazz tradition.[18]Late 1960s and 1970seditTaylor began to perform solo concerts in the latter half of the 1960s. The first known recorded solo performance was "Carmen With Rings" (59 minutes) in De Doelen concert hall in Rotterdam on July 1, 1967. Two days earlier, Taylor had played the same composition in the Amsterdam Concertgebouw. Many of his later concerts were released on album and include Indent (1973), side one of Spring of Two Blue-J's (1973), Silent Tongues (1974), Garden (1982), For Olim (1987), Erzulie Maketh Scent (1989), and The Tree of Life (1998).[19] He began to garner critical and popular acclaim, playing for Jimmy Carter on the White House Lawn,[20] lecturing as an artist-in-residence at universities, and eventually being awarded a Guggenheim Fellowship in 1973.[21]In 1976, Taylor directed a production of Adrienne Kennedy's A Rat's Mass at La MaMa Experimental Theatre Club in the East Village of Manhattan. His production combined the original script with a chorus of orchestrated voices used as instruments. Jimmy Lyons, Rashid Bakr, Andy Bey, Karen Borca, David S. Ware and Raphe Malik performed in the production as the Cecil Taylor Unit, among other musicians and actors.[22]1980s, 1990s, and the Feel TrioeditFollowing Lyons' death in 1986, Taylor formed the Feel Trio in the late 1980s with William Parker on bass and Tony Oxley on drums. The group can be heard on Celebrated Blazons, Looking (Berlin Version) The Feel Trio and the 10-disc set 2 Ts for a Lovely T.[23][24][25] Compared to his prior groups with Lyons, the Feel Trio had a more abstract approach, tethered less to jazz tradition and more aligned with the ethos of European free improvisation. He also performed with larger ensembles and big band projects.Taylor's extended residence in Berlin in 1988 was documented by the German label FMP, resulting in a box set of performances in duet and trio with a large number of European free improvisors, including Oxley, Derek Bailey, Evan Parker, Han Bennink, Tristan Honsinger, Louis Moholo, and Paul Lovens. Most of his later recordings have been released on European labels, with the exception of Momentum Space (a meeting with Dewey Redman and Elvin Jones) on Verve/Gitanes. The classical label Bridge released his 1998 Library of Congress performance Algonquin, a duet with violinist Mat Maneri.[26]Taylor continued to perform for capacity audiences around the world with live concerts, usually playing his favored instrument, a Bösendorfer piano featuring nine extra lower-register keys. In 1987, he toured England with Australian pianist Roger Woodward, presenting recitals on which Woodward played solo works by Xenakis, Takemitsu, and Feldman, followed by Taylor, also playing solo.[27] A documentary on Taylor, entitled All the Notes, was released on DVD in 2006 by director Chris Felver. Taylor was also featured in a 1981 documentary film entitled Imagine the Sound, in which he discusses and performs his music, poetry, and dance.[28] In 1993, he was awarded a MacArthur Fellowship.[29][30]2000seditCecil Taylor, Buffalo, New YorkTaylor recorded sparingly in the 2000s, but continued to perform with his own ensembles (the Cecil Taylor Ensemble and the Cecil Taylor Big Band) and with other musicians such as Joe Locke, Max Roach, and Amiri Baraka.[31] In 2004, the Cecil Taylor Big Band at the Iridium Jazz Club was nominated a best performance of 2004 by All About Jazz.[32] The Cecil Taylor Trio was nominated for the same at the Highline Ballroom in 2009.[33] The trio consisted of Taylor, Albey Balgochian, and Jackson Krall. In 2010, Triple Point Records released a deluxe limited-edition double LP titled Ailanthus/Altissima: Bilateral Dimensions of 2 Root Songs, a set of duos with Taylor's longtime collaborator Tony Oxley that was recorded live at the Village Vanguard.[34]In 2013, he was awarded the Kyoto Prize for Music.[35] He was described as "An Innovative Jazz Musician Who Has Fully Explored the Possibilities of Piano Improvisation".[36] In 2014, his career and 85th birthday were honored at the Painted Bride Art Center in Philadelphia with the tribute concert event "Celebrating Cecil".[37] In 2016, Taylor received a retrospective at the Whitney Museum of American Art entitled "Open Plan: Cecil Taylor".[38]In 2008, Taylor performed with Pauline Oliveros at the Curtis R Priem Experimental Media and Performing Arts Center at Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute. The concert was recorded and is available on a DVD which also features a 75-minute video of a Taylor poetry recital entitled Floating Gardens: The Poetry Of Cecil Taylor.[39][40] Taylor, along with dancer Min Tanaka, was the subject of Amiel Courtin-Wilson's 2016 documentary film The Silent Eye.[41]Ballet and danceeditIn addition to piano, Taylor was always interested in ballet and dance. His mother, who died while he was young, was a dancer and played the piano and violin. Taylor once said: "I try to imitate on the piano the leaps in space a dancer makes."[42] He collaborated with dancer Dianne McIntyre from the mid 1970s to the early 1980s.[43] In 1979, he composed and played the music for a 12-minute ballet, "Tetra Stomp: Eatin' Rain in Space", featuring Mikhail Baryshnikov and Heather Watts.[44]PoetryeditTaylor was a poet, and cited Robert Duncan, Charles Olson, and Amiri Baraka as major influences.[45] He often integrated his poems into his musical performances, and they frequently appear in the liner notes of his albums. The album Chinampas, released by Leo Records in 1987, is a recording of Taylor reciting several of his poems while accompanying himself on percussion.[46] His poetry was likened to his music primarily by the ways in which Taylor alters and transforms material both linguistic and musical.[47]Musical style and legacyeditAccording to Steven Block, free jazz originated with Taylor's performances at the Five Spot Cafe in 1957 and with Ornette Coleman in 1959.[48] In 1964, Taylor co-founded the Jazz Composers Guild to enhance opportunities for avant-garde jazz musicians.[49]Taylor's style and methods have been described as "constructivist".[50] Despite Scott Yanow's warning regarding Taylor's "forbidding music" ("Suffice it to say that Cecil Taylor's music is not for everyone"), he praises Taylor's "remarkable technique and endurance", and his "advanced", "radical", "original", and uncompromising "musical vision".[5]This musical vision is a large part of Taylor's legacy:Playing with Taylor I began to be liberated from thinking about chords. I'd been imitating John Coltrane unsuccessfully and because of that I was really chord conscious.— Archie Shepp, quoted in LeRoi Jones, album liner notes for Four for Trane (Impulse A-71, 1964)Scott Yanow of AllMusic wrote: "Taylor's high-energy atonalism fit in well with the free jazz of the period but he was actually leading the way rather than being part of a movement. [...] In fact, it could be safely argued that no jazz music of the era approached the ferocity and intensity of Cecil Taylor's."[51]Personal life and deatheditTaylor moved to Fort Greene, Brooklyn, in 1983.[9] He died at his Brooklyn residence on April 5, 2018, at the age of 89.[52][53] At the time of his death, Taylor was working on an autobiography and future concerts, among other projects.[54]DiscographyeditMain article: Cecil Taylor discographyReferencesedit^ Such, David Glen (1993). Avant-garde Jazz Musicians: Performing "Out There". items.body: ＜Artist Interview＞ Akane SAKAI Eine Pianistin, die Menschen verbindet und Räume erschafft text by Hiroyuki YAGI translation by Prof. em. Kazumi SAKAI Cover Photo by Andrej GRILC Die Begegnung mit Argerich Die Pianistin Akane SAKAI schloss ihr Studium an der Toho Gakuen University ab und ging anschließend nach Belgien. Seither ist Brüssel der Ausgangspunkt ihrer internationalen Karriere. Sie tritt als Solistin bei Musikfestivals, in Konzertsälen und mit Orchestern auf der ganzen Welt auf. Besonders geprägt wurde ihre künstlerische Laufbahn durch die enge Zusammenarbeit mit Martha Argerich. Von einer der bedeutendsten Pianistinnen der Nachkriegszeit mit großem Vertrauen bedacht, ist Sakai nicht nur Argerichs Partnerin für Duo- und vierhändige Aufführungen, sondern für die künstlerische Planung des „Argerich Festivals“ in Hamburg verantwortlich. Durch diese Zusammenarbeit wurde ihr Name vielen Musikliebhabern und -liebhaberinnen bekannt. Doch wie verlief ihr künstlerischer Werdegang? Um den Mensch hinter dem Namen näher kennenzulernen, sprachen wir ausführlich mit Akane SAKAI. Sakai begegnete Argerich zum ersten Mal, als sie im Abschlussjahrgang des Toho Gakuen Musikgymnasiums für Mädchen war. „Ich war ein großer Argerich-Fan. Nach jedem Konzert, das ich besuchte, stellte ich mich in die Schlange für ein Autogramm. Irgendwann schien Martha mein Gesicht wiederzuerkennen. Eines Tages fragte sie mich: ‚Du studierst doch Klavier, oder? Möchtest du mir einmal vorspielen?’ Ich antwortete natürlich, dass ich das sehr gerne tun würde – war aber ehrlich gesagt nicht sicher, ob Martha es wirklich ernst meinte. Doch sie wollte mich tatsächlich spielen hören. Damals wohnte ich noch im Wohnheim der Toho Gakuen , als mich jemand von KAJIMOTO anrief und sagte, Martha sei gerade in Hamamatsuchō, um Instrumente auszuwählen und ich solle dorthin kommen. Martha mag keinen Regen, und an diesem Tag regnete es und ihre Laune war entsprechend getrübt. Schließlich hörte sie mir im Tokyo Metropolitan Theatre zu – kurz vor ihrem Konzert mit Gidon Kremer. Für mich war es wie ein Traum, vor der Pianistin zu spielen, die ich so sehr bewunderte. Ich war so aufgeregt und glücklich, dass ich mich kaum noch daran erinnere, wie ich gespielt habe. Danach lud sie mich sogar noch zum Essen ein. So begann meine besondere, fast unglaubliche Verbindung zu Martha.” Nach ihrem Studienabschluss der Toho Gakuen University ging Sakai nach Belgien. Auch bei der Wahl dieses Studienortes hatte Argerich sie aufmerksam und herzlich unterstützt. „Ursprünglich hatte ich geplant, in Deutschland zu studieren, doch der Professor, bei dem ich lernen wollte, war inzwischen in den Ruhestand gegangen, sodass ich meinen Plan noch einmal überdenken musste. Als ich Martha um Rat fragte, empfahl sie mir das Königliche Konservatorium Brüssel. Auf ihre Empfehlung hin entschied ich mich für Belgien. Am Königlichen Konservatorium Brüssel studierte Sakai bei Evgeny Mogilevsky und am Conservatorium SLAC in Leuven bei Alan Weiss, wo sie ihr Diplom mit Auszeichnung abschloss. Seitdem ist mir Brüssel sehr ans Herz gewachsen“, erklärt sie. „Die Stadt ist mein Ausgangspunkt geblieben. Brüssel ist eine sehr kosmopolitische Stadt, in der viele ausländische Musiker und Musikerinnen leben – unter ihnen die Geigerin Yuzuko HORIGOME. Außerdem ist die Lage ideal: Frankreich, Deutschland und die Niederlande sind in kürzester Zeit zu erreichen. Auch für Martha war Brüssel einer ihrer Lebensmittelpunkte. Sie war häufig in der Stadt.” Akane SAKAI ©︎Andrej GRILC Als künstlerische Partnerin Der Kontakt zu Argerich brach auch nach Sakais Studienzeit in Belgien nicht ab. Im Gegenteil: aus der Beziehung der beiden entwickelte sich mit der Zeit eine einer echten künstlerische Partnerschaft. „Auch nach meinem Studium habe ich Martha regelmäßig zu Hause vorgespielt. Sie ist unglaublich bescheid en und gibt ihre Ratschläge immer sehr vorsichtig und behutsam. Unser erster gemeinsamer Auftritt war, soweit ich mich erinnere, 2005 beim Argerich Festival in Buenos Aires statt – dort haben wir vierhändig Schubert und Ravel gespielt. Danach sind wir auch beim Festival in Lugano gemeinsam aufgetreten. Neben unseren Duo-Auftritten und dem vierhändigen Spiel bin ich seit dem Beginn des Argerich Festivals in Hamburg im Jahr 2018 auch als künstlerische Planerin tätig.” Argerich umgibt eine Aura, die selbst unter großen Pianistinnen außergewöhnlich ist. Wie erlebt Sakai, die ihr seit langer Zeit sehr nahe ist, diese Ausnahmekünstlerin? „Martha und ich hatten von Anfang an ein sehr vertrautes Verhältnis. Daran hat sich auch nichts geändert, als wir gemeinsam auf der Bühne standen. Als musikalische Partnerin führt Martha das Spiel, aber sie tut das auf eine Weise, die das Beste aus ihren Mitspielern und Mitspielerinnen holt. Sie drängt sich nicht in den Vordergrund, zieht sich aber auch nicht zurück. Dieses feine Gleichgewicht findet sie ganz instinktiv. Vor allem aber begegnet Martha allen Menschen auf Augenhöhe. Bei den Festivals in Lugano und Hamburg erhalten alle Beteiligten dasselbe Honorar, sie legt keinen Wert auf Sonderbehandlung. Als ich Martha kennenlernte, war sie Anfang fünfzig. Ich glaube, sie ist seither deutlich gelassener geworden. Früher mochte sie es gar nicht, wenn bei Interviews Kameras liefen. Heute schaut sie mit Begeisterung YouTube-Videos und stört sich kaum noch daran, gefilmt zu werden.” Akane SAKAI mit Martha Argerich und Stephen Kovacevich, Lucerne. Sakais Mission als künstlerische Planerin Wie bereits erwähnt, ist Sakai beim jährlich im Juni in Hamburg stattfindenden Argerich Festival für die künstlerische Planung verantwortlich, eine Aufgabe, die einmal mehr zeigt, wie groß das Vertrauen ist, das Argerich in sie setzt. Doch was genau umfasst diese Rolle? „Das Festival wird von den Hamburger Symphonikern veranstaltet. Deshalb stimme ich mich eng mit dem Intendanten des Orchesters ab und entscheide gemeinsam mit ihm über Besetzung und Programm. Mein Schwerpunkt liegt vor allem auf den Rezitals und der Kammermusik außerhalb der Orchesterkonzerte. 2026 findet das Festival vom 20. bis 30. Juni statt, und Japan wird eines der Leitthemen sein. Im Zentrum steht die Europapremiere von Dai FUJIKURAs Klavierkonzert Nr. 4 „Akiko’s Piano“, bei der ich als Solistin auftreten werde. Akiko KAWAMOTO, die beim Atombombenabwurf auf Hiroshima ums Leben kam, wäre 2026 hundert Jahre alt geworden; auch das Pianino, das sie so sehr liebte, feiert in diesem Jahr seinen hundertsten Geburtstag. Ursprünglich war Martha als Solistin der Uraufführung vorgesehen. Wegen der Einreisebeschränkungen während der Corona-Pandemie war das leider nicht möglich. Das ist einer der Gründe, weshalb wir das Werk nun in Hamburg aufführen. Akikos Klavier selbst kann nicht nach Europe gebracht werden, weil die Tasten Elfenbein enthalten und aufgrund internationaler Artenschutzbestimmungen auch nicht für kurze Zeit das Land verlassen können. Die Firma Casio hat den Klang des Instruments jedoch digitalisiert, und in der Kadenz der Hamburger Aufführung werde ich dieses digitalisierte Klavier verwenden. Darüber hinaus ist eine Aufführung des Noh-Stücks „Postman of Nagasaki“ von Shōnosuke ŌKURA geplant, der sowohl Noh-Schauspieler als auch Ōtsuzumi*-Spieler ist. Das Werk basiert auf Peter Townsends Roman „The Postman of Nagasaki“ und wurde 2025, zum achtzigsten Jahrestag des Kriegsendes, als Noh-Stück aufgeführt. Gemeinsam mit Fujikuras Werk gibt es dem Festivalpublikum die Möglichkeit, über Frieden und nukleare Abrüstung nachzudenken. Beim Argerich Festival in Hamburg legen wir großen Wert auf ein vielfältiges Programm: Neben japanischem Noh-Theater bringen wir ganz bewusst Musik aus aller Welt auf die Bühne – Jazz, indische Musik, Flamenco und vieles mehr.” Auch bei der Auswahl der klassischen Mitwirkenden spürt man Sakais tiefes Verständnis für den Geist Argerichs. „Uns ist es wichtig, eine gute Balance zu finden, zwischen den Künstlerinnen und Künstlern, die Martha seit vielen Jahren begleiten, und solchen, die zum ersten Mal beim Festival dabei sind werden. So entsteht ein Programm, das man wirklich nur in Hamburg erleben kann – ohne vorhersehbarer Routine. Natürlich bereiten wir auch Aufführungen vor, die man unbedingt mit Martha hören möchte, etwa sämtliche Violinsonaten von Beethoven gespielt von Martha und Maxim Vengerov. Ein weiterer Bestandteil des Festivals ist unsere Reihe mit Schumann-Liedern, für die wir jedes Jahr eine andere Sängerin oder einen anderen Sänger einladen. Man könnte sagen: So wie Rudolf Serkin beim Marlboro Music Festival immer wieder Beethovens Fantasie für Klavier, Chor und Orchester aufführte, ist diese Schumann-Reihe inzwischen zu einem Symbol des Argerich Festivals in Hamburg geworden. Das Festival in Hamburg – und das gilt auch für das Tokioter Festival „La Folle Journée“, bei dem ich häufig mitwirke – ist von einer sehr familiären Atmosphäre geprägt. Die Künstlerinnen und Künstler sollen das Gefühl haben, nach Hause zurückzukehren. Dass alle Beteiligten einander auf Augenhöhe begegnen und echtes Vertrauen zueinander aufbauen: Das ist das Allerwichtigste für Martha.” *Ōtsuzumi, eine Trommel, die in der klassischen japanischen Musik verwendet wird. Akane SAKAI mit Daniel Kühnel, Intendant des Hamburger Symphoniker. Die Wiederentdeckung der »Jahreszeiten« Ein weiteres bemerkenswertes Projekt Sakais ist die monatliche Veröffentlichung einzelnen Stücks aus Tschaikowskys Klavierzyklus »Die Jahreszeiten« auf YouTube. „Der Anstoß dazu kam durch ein Konzert beim Lausitz Festival in Görlitz im September 2022“, erzählt Sakai. „Dort spielte ich Tschaikowskys „Jahreszeiten“, begleitet von einer Lesung aus Erich Kästners Gedichtzyklus „Die 13 Monate“. Japanische Leser und Leserinnen kennen Kästner sicher als den Autor des Kinderbuchs „Das doppelte Lottchen“. Die Aufführung hatte zudem eine szenische Komponente: Aus einem sogenannten Osmodrama strömten passend zu den Gedichten Düfte in den Zuschauerraum. Durch diese Erfahrung habe ich die „Jahreszeiten“ für mich neu entdeckt und habe das Werk seither immer wieder in meine Rezitalprogramme aufgenommen. Da sich 2026 die Erstveröffentlichung von Tschaikowskys „Jahreszeiten“, zum 150. Mal jährt, hat Sakai beschlossen, dieses Jubiläum mit einem besonderen Projekt zu feiern. Jeden Monat veröffentlicht sie ein Stück aus dem Zyklus auf YouTube. Ursprünglich erschienen die „Jahreszeiten“ als monatliche Beilage einer Musikzeitschrift. Für Sakai sind sie ein Meisterwerk, in die feinsinnige Musikalität des russischen Komponisten in ihrer ganzen Fülle erfahrbar wird. „Tschaikowskys Werke für Soloklavier sind noch immer vergleichsweise wenig bekannt“, sagt sie. „Dabei gibt es neben den „Jahreszeiten“ viele verborgene Schätze, etwa die ‚18 Morceaux‘ (op. 72). Auch diese Werke möchte ich in Zukunft mit großer Sorgfalt pflegen.” Akane SAKAI mit „Osmodrama“ beim Lausitz Festival 2022. Ein Rezital in ihrer Heimatstadt Nagoya Am 6. Juni gibt Sakai in ihrer Heimstadt Nagoya ein Rezital in der Konzerthalle Runde. „In Nagoya habe ich 2025 eine jährliche Rezital-Reihe ins Leben gerufen. Beim zweiten Konzert stehen neben Werken von Chopin, Skrjabin und Beethoven auch Dai FUJIKURAs „Akiko’s Diary for piano“ auf dem Programm. Dieses Stück ist eine eigenständige Fassung der Kadenz aus dem bereits erwähnten Fujikuras Klavierkonzert Nr. 4. Auch in Nagoya werde ich Akikos digitalisiertes Klavier verwenden. In dieser Reihe nehme ich jedes Jahr ein Werk eines lebenden Komponisten ins Programm auf; im vergangenen Jahr spielte ich eine Etüde von Toshio HOSOKAWA. Darüber hinaus verbinde ich in meinem Rezital Werke von Skrjabin mit Musik seines großen Vorbilds Chopin. Skrjabin gilt zwar oft als schwer zugänglich, doch seine Musik ist eigentlich von großer Schönheit und unmittelbarer Ausdruckskraft. Ich bin überzeugt, dass auch Menschen, die Skrjabin noch nicht kennen, seine Musik genießen können. Das Programm vereint Chopins Fantasie f–Moll op. 49, Skrjabins 2. Klaviersonate Gis-Moll op. 19, Beethovens Fantasiefür Klavier in H-Dur op. 77 und seine Klaviersonate Nr. 32 in c-Moll op. 111 – ein Abend der ganz im Zeichen musikalischer Vorstellungskraft steht. Ich freue mich sehr darauf, das Publikum in Nagoya begrüßen zu dürfen“, sagt Sakai. Wie unser Gespräch zeigt, ist Sakai eine Künstlerin mit weitem Horizont und klarer Vision. Inspiriert von Martha Argerich, verließ sie Japan und hat sich seither nicht nur als Pianistin, sondern auch als Produzentin das Vertrauen von Künstlerinnen und Künstlern aus aller Welt erworben. Mit ihrer Fähigkeit, durch Musik Menschen miteinander zu verbinden und neue Räume zu schaffen, hat sie der klassischen Musikszene wichtige Impulse gegeben. In Japan waren die Gelegenheiten, Sakai live zu erleben bislang begrenzt. Künftig möchte Sakai die Konzerttätigkeit in ihrem Heimatland jedoch weiter auszubauen und die Erfahrung, die sie über viele Jahre hinweg gesammelt hat, an jüngere Generationen weitergeben. Wir werden Sakais unkonventionellen musikalischen Weg auch in Zukunft weiterhin aufmerksam begleiten. Akane SAKAI ©︎Andrej GRILC Akane SAKAI Die in Nagoya geborene Pianistin Akane SAKAI lernte zunächst am Toho Gakuen Musikgymnasium für Mädchen und später an der Toho Gakuen University unter Midori MIURA. Anschließend setzte sie ihre Ausbildung in Belgien fort:am Königlichen Konservatorium Brüssel bei Evgeny Mogilevsky sowie am Conservatorium SLAC in Leuven bei Alan Weiss, wo mit Auszeichnung, dem Premier Prix, abschloss. Weitere künstlerische Impulse erhielt sie von Pavel Gililov und Lilya Zilberstein. Sakai war Stipendiatin der NPO Yellow Angel, des Program of Overseas Study for Upcoming Artists des japanischen Amts für kulturelle Angelegenheiten*. Als Solitistin arbeitete sie mit zahlreichen renommierten Orchestern zusammen, darunter die Kremerata Baltica, Sinfonia Varsovia, die Symphoniker Hamburg, das Orchestre national Avignon-Provence, das Orchestra della Svizzera italiana, das Tokyo Symphony Orchestra, die Manchester Camerata, und das Orchestre de Chambre de Lausanne. Zu den Dirigenten, mit denen sie musizierte, zählen Alexander Vedernikov, Sylvain Cambreling, Lionel Bringuier, Jean-Jacques Kantorow, Hubert Soudant und Naoto ŌTOMO. Regelmäßig ist Akane Sakai bei internationalen Musikfestivals zu Gast, unter anderem bei La Folle Journée in Nantes und Tokio, dem Pacific Music Festival in Sapporo), dem Festival La Roque-d’Anthéron, dem polnischen Festival „Chopin und sein Europa“ (Polen), dem Lausitz Festival, dem Festival Lugano und dem Beppu Argerich Festival in Japan. Ihr Repertoire spannt einen weiten Bogen von Bach bis zur Musik des 20. und 21. Jahrhunderts. Neben Werken von Prokofjew, Bartók, Messiaen und Takemitsu widmet sie sich auch selten gespielten Kompositionen von Władysław Szpilman, Roman Maciejewski und Mieczysław Weinberg. Eine besondere Rolle spielt in Sakais künstlerischer Arbeit die Kammermusik. Sie tritt regelmäßig mit herausragenden Musikern und Musikerinnen wie Martha Argerich, Gidon Kremer, Ivry Gitlis, Yuzuko HORIGOME, Nicholas Angelich, Alexander Knyazev, Mayu KISHIMA, Evgeni Bozhanov und Yoshiko KAWAMOTO auf. Ihre Aufnahmen erschienen unter anderem bei Warner Music, der Deutschen Grammophon – darunter Live-Aufnahmen ihrer Auftritte auf dem Festival Lugano – sowie bei King International. Ihre erste Solo-CD „Strawinsky, Prokofjew, Ravel“ wurde von der japanischen Fachzeitschrift Record Geijutsu als herausragende Einspielung ausgezeichnet. Ihre jüngste Aufnahme „Voyages“, erschien im Juni 2022 beim deutschen Label Acousence. Neben ihrer Konzerttätigkeit ist Akane SAKAI für die künsterlische Planung des Martha Argerich Festivals Hamburg verantwortlich. Sie engagiert sich zudem als Jurorin internationaler Wettbewerbe, als Dozentin bei Meisterklassen und als Autorin. *Sonderamt unter dem Ministerium für Bildung, Kultur, Sport, Wissenschaft und Technologie. Offizielle Website: https://www.akanesakai.com/ YouTube: https://youtube.com/@akaneconcert7781 Martha Argerich Festival Hamburg: https://www.symphonikerhamburg.de/martha-argerich-festival

items.body: Ghent brass band Brazzmatazz was formed in 2014, released their debut EP in 2015, expanded to a 12-piece band for their first album in 2018, released a live set in 2021 and is now even larger, an 18-strong leviathan. Whenever someone buys their music, each member will receive only a pittance, so they hope people purchase a lot! The album’s first single and video appeared last year; for an upbeat band, they are certainly in no hurry. Clockwork Concerto intersperses scenes of the band dressing for a concert, donning outfits that look like something from a cyberpunk Renn Faire, creating a giant clock wheel, and performing in front of an eager, bouncy audience. Various members take their time to shine, starting with a sax solo and continuing with a slow, jazzy trumpet interlude. Before long, everyone is dancing again, on stage and off. Second single “Walk the Plank” is where the band captured our attention; the video was featured in our Spring Music Preview. Here the band’s ebullience is on full display as they dress up, act out and take a tour of the docks, to the delight (and perhaps slight befuddlement) of passers-by. In the Bandcamp liner notes, Brazzamatazz goes full-on pirate. There’s a touch of Madness in the visuals, while the timbre will appeal to fans of The Mighty Mighty Bosstones, The Hippos and Reel Big Fish. The shouts of “Walk the Plank” may lead to the song becoming a TikTok sensation; we certainly hope so (and it would help to feed the band, who uses up a lot of calories). There’s a plaintive breakdown after all but two are arrested, the leftovers drifting away slowly as a duo. But wait, there’s more! Crank Up the Pressure jumps right in with the chanty, handclappy title track, a party song if we’ve ever heard one (“Ho! Hey! Ya!”). Sometimes two players get solos at once; with a band this big, there’s no avoiding it. “Fistycuffs” has the feel of a play fight between good friends, faking the tension for an audience. The Bond-esque “Ocular Phenomenon” breaks down to expose a bank of cheers, while “Losbandigheid” begins with laughter and showcases a bongo solo before doubling its tempo and halving it again. Everyone is having a literal blast. Due to their contagious energy, we can see Brazzmatazz being a huge concert attraction. “Puppet Play” seems like the obvious choice for a third single, due to its eight-note earworm, wordless bar room singalong, numerous tempo changes and happy handclaps. What else does one need as the summer starts and one finds time to hang out with one’s mates? “Barrage” may appeal to fans of A Comet Is Coming, helping the band to cross over to yet another audience. This may end up being the happiest album of the year. (Richard Allen)

items.body: Derek Jarman award-winner and Turner Prize nominee Luke Fowler speaks to Claire M. Holdsworth about his latest film, A Sensation Never Yet Known, a portrait of the electroacoustic composer and musician Janet Beat Merging art and documentary, the films of Glasgow-based artist and musician Luke Fowler examine people who are dismissed, marginalised or mis-recognised in their time. From psychiatrist R.D. Laing and Marxist historian E.P. Thompson to Orcadian filmmaker Margaret Tait, Fowler’s 16mm film portraits expose the process of making and researching them. Combining sounds and images in ways that resist narrative storytelling, his works often present snapshot encounters with the lives and work of visionary composers, like Martin Bartlett, Cornelius Cardew, Brunhild Ferrari and Christian Wolff. Fowler and I speak on... The post Dancing on Moonbeams: Artist Luke Fowler on Electronic Music Pioneer Janet Beat appeared first on The Quietus.

items.body: Review by siLLy puPPy — The Portuguese prog scene was already late to the game once the Carnation Revolution of 1974 usheredin the era of artistic and musical freedom however the Iberian Peninsula had a few years to sow itswild prog oats before succumbing to the same financial pressures faced by all the 70s bands. Aftertwo lauded prog albums that topped the scene in terms of talent and innovation, TANTRA made one ofthe most dramatic decisions of its career and jumped ship from the prog train altogether. Well,what's a has-been prog band to do? Either break up altogether and disappear into the ethers or dowhat many others did which is channel their inner Ultravox, Tubeway Army and Duran Duran and jointhe party that punk rock started and all its derivatives developed along the way. Introducing thenew TANTRA, a bonfide new wave act that discovered a newfound fascination with the Coneheads!Needless to say this went over as well as liver-flavored pop tarts at a moppet's birthday partydespite the band proving to have a real knack for a ridiculously clever and catchy display ofsynthpop-infused new wave that sounded as if it was part Talking Heads, Thomas Dolby and perhapsOingo Boingo at least in terms of that exaggerated vocal style. While many prog bands that went thisdirection failed miserably in trying to emulate their fish out of water approach to making musicthat was as alien to them as a clutch of captured grays in Area 51, TANTRA was surprisingly adept atcrafting infectiously addictive pop hooks that delivered interesting guitar work, above averagedrumming for the style and a beautiful tapestry of synthesized atmospheric touches. Add to that theband delivers nine distinct tracks that offered an album of some top notch new wave of the era. Andlove the thumpin' bass grooves!As bouncy as the B52s and as hook-laden as Peter Schilling, TANTRA showed absolutely zero sign thatits previous album was a knotty progressive powerhouse of complexity making this one of the mostdramatic transitions in all of prog history as far as i know since the modus operandi of most bandswas to slowly morph into the 80s pop era rather than jump in head first. Despite this bold displayof sallying forth into the brave new world, TANTRA didn't miss a beat and did its homework asbeautifully regarding the new wave style as it did for prog. While the production on this one is alittle weak and because it was such a bomb as far as sales were concerned, the album has never beenreissued much less remastered but from a musical point of view, HUMANOID FLESH is a stellar exampleof early 80s new wave, a style of music that i find extremely appealing and since i don't compareband's album and rate them on their own merits, i'm happy to say that this is instantly lovable slabof new wave ready for MTV primetime. Unfortunately the prog fans despised this music at the time and new wave fans would not warm up to aprog band crashing the party so the band would've been much better of rebranding itself as ThePortuguese Pigeons or something rather than continuing on as TANTRA therefore the results are aridiculously low rating for this album that under any other name would've been well regarded as anew wave release of the day. I've listened to countless new wave albums from the 70s and 80s andthere are very few where every track is great so it's ironic that this almost universally hatedrelease is so friggin' good and i don't mean just OK. I really love every track on this one andalthough it's very easy to hear the influences on board, TANTRA does an admirable job of making itall their own. I was quite surprised that this has quickly emerged as one of my favorite new wavealbums of the 80s! Gimme both prog TANTRA and new wave TANTRA. I'm that kinda music freak ~ haha!

items.body: Review by siLLy puPPy — TANTRA emerged on the Portuguese prog scene in 1977 with its critically acclaimed debut "Mist�rios eMaravilhas" which mined the elaborately complex world of English symphonic prog ranging from Yes andGenesis to Camel and the Italian scene with lyrics in the native Portuguese language however in ayear's time the band experienced a few changes. Firstly keyboardist Pedro Luis jumped on board andoccupied the vacant seat left by the departure of Armando Gama and the band welcomed two guests:guitarist and vocalist Tony Moura and keyboardist Pedro Mestre to contribute to the more complexstyle that featured a new jump in ingenuity that displayed a jazz fusion mesh underlining in thealready spectacular performances of the symphonic prog that graced the debut.HOLOCAUSTO emerged in 1978 and took TANTRA'S prog excesses even further into the realms of crazycomplexities with six tracks that challenged the listener in the vein of some of the moreadventurous albums of the genre yet retaining much of the accessible features that kept it fromgetting too avant-garde for its own good. With extended influences from fusion acts like MahavishnuOrchestra, Soft Machine and others as well as maintaining the Portuguese folk sensibilities,HOLOCAUSTO was the crushing pinnacle of the ferocity and ingenuity of the Portuguese prog scenewhich showcases melodic vocal-led passages as well as crafty prog workouts that exhibited varyingstylistic shifts, tempo changes and wild hairpin turns that somehow maintained a continuity on thetracks where they were implemented. The musicians were well oiled machines at this point and in manyways this album blew away the competition except for perhaps the short-lived act Saga which releasedone equally adventurous and challenging album.The album opens with the more pacifying "Om" which doesn't stray too far from the band's symphonicprog beginnings with a style that emulates the in-between zone of Yes and Genesis however beginningwith the second track which is a two-part masterwork, "Holocausto / �ltimo Raio do Astro Rei" takesthings into prog paradise with unthinkably clever excursions into varying themes and musicaldevelopments and allows the band members to pull out their fanciest chops that display some of themost talented musicians of the entire 70s Portuguese prog scene. This particular track walks theperfect tightrope act between symphonic prog sensibilities and high wire jazz fusion gymnasticsoffering a satisfying display of pompous prog run amok, my favorite kind! Add to that escapistjourneys into space rock and even moments of raga and it's easy to qualify this as one of the bestprog tracks of the entire 70s. The rest of the album is equally stunning with "Talism�" following suit and then "Ara" jumping intoslower space rock territory and then sounding more like something like the Alan Parsons Projectwould conjure up with piano-driven lyric based a sing-songy although laced more in Camel keyboardelegance. "Ji" ends it all with a more commercial sound more indicative of the 1978 timeline withthat famous crossover sound of bands like Styx or Sumpertramp but slightly proggier. This is aparticularly excellent release with some of the best progressive rock of the era however the albumseems inconsistent in its style and the ability to string it all together without sounding forcedand at least for my liking, the vocalist also feels a bit clunky at times so even though i wouldn'tdeem this a perfect album it certainly has some bouts with genius on it. This was the end ofTANTRA's prog career and to the fan's chagrin the band sallied forth in full new wave mode on itsfollowup "Humanoid Flesh" which would provide a fatal move on the band's part which would soon breakup afterwards.

Much of this is instrumental, with elements of Gryphon and Camel in particular as they combine folk elements with traditional and Neo prog, but for some weird reason it is an album I have found incredibly difficult to warm to.I have no idea why, as it contains much I enjoy about progressive rock music, yet there seems very little in the way of soul and heart, and it feels much more like a clinical project as opposed to a band. It is all very clever, with clean presentation, broad use of different instrumentation, and there is no doubt all involved are highly skilled, yet it just doesn't grab me like it should. I note that opinions are incredibly varied, with some listeners treating this as the finest offering since sliced bread, while others feel it is stale and just do not understand what all the fuss is about. I guess I am somewhat in the middle, as I really want to rave over this as in many ways, I feel it deserves it, yet there is no spark and whenever I finish playing it there is no huge desire to put it on again. They say beauty is in the ear of the beholder, or something like that, so all I can say is that it is worth hearing and you may feel it is a hidden gem, but don't be surprised if it is also just a lump of rock.

items.body: Review by tszirmay — Third album for these 'ambient-jazz" pioneers from Italy , their previous work was a smashing success that I reviewed and thus enjoyed tremendously. As expresses in my review for "Trans-Neptunian Objects", this quartet has sculpted a rather unique stylistic that bodes well for its ongoing career, having offered only a very distant comparison to the legendary Weather Report (mostly due to Andrea Serino's crafty e-piano work). Well, why not dwell on a winning recipe, as the Fender Rhodes plays an even more significant role here , much to my personal delight and surely yours as well! The same talented crew is back for another thrilling adventure that deserves your attention. Andrea Grumelli tackles the fretless bass challenges with overt glee, in complete synchronicity with kitman Matteo Ravelli. Guitarist Andrea Ferrari also experiments with keyboards (as well as a few prancing horses, I presume), shouldering the previously highlighted Serino clever fingers). Six demanding tracks for 43 minutes of listening joy. The first overriding sensation on "Oort Cloud" is one of immersive mind music, acting like a gentle sonic anaesthetic before flicking a switch that plunges the unexpecting listener into near Magma-esque orbit, the illuminated piano remaining the sole melodic component while the remaining instruments behave more like percussive beasts, let loose to rampage. Cubic obliqueness is up next , as if Pablo Picasso suddenly was given the baton to lead the orchestra into experimental dissonance that nevertheless has tons of shape, with Salvador Dali doing gargoyle voices on the savage "Vogon". Thankfully Andrea Ferrari takes his raging Testarossa guitar into overdrive, full throttle down the autostrada, the hell with the stunned Carabinieri left in the lurch. In the paddock, Grumelli, Serino and Ravelli waltz around the clock, impishly smiling like kids in a playground. Highlight core tracks happen to own French language titles (winking at the Aosta valley from nearby Milan) first with the luxuriant "Cinq Teintes, Quatre Cadres", a sublime piece that should hypnotize anyone into submission. Grumelli once gain sets the hue and the team willingly follow, painting the air with an assortment of vivid strokes that define the word palette. Screeching guitars, pugnacious drums and keyboard-driven fireworks maintain the balance between gliding serenely and dive-bombing. The glittering piano acts as the surrealist spine, distributing insistent cords/cards like a dealer in Las Vegas. The distant electronics add a neo-modern sheen that cannot be overlooked either. ''La M�lancolie du Petit Prince'' refers explicitly to the classic Antoine de St-Exup�ry novel, a much cherish literary legend that keeps the spirit alive. The grand piano takes the center stage, offering a classical modus operandi, the chattering percussive talking up a storm, while the voluptuous bass guitar does its cobra-like slithering in the desert, among the sonic dunes. The billion stars shape the dark sky as one questions the reason for our existence and the unpredictable fate that awaits each adventurer. Antoine did and then wrote a book. You, the listener will remember and revisit all the music moments that impact your soul. Aether bridge the distance between classical music and prog and await imminent rescue.As per its definition, "Panta Rei" is a flowing river of constant change, an evolutive expression that, with the right amount of attention and appreciation, can take you wherever you dare to dream. Ferrari's fretboard excursion is a not only ferociously intense but can veer easily into another world altogether, recalling perhaps a vision of an emerald beyond or even fiery fowls. Serino has his spot as well and takes full advantage of the limelight to seal the deal. The nearly 11 minute "Swerve " closes the proverbial book on this third offering, a very a propos title, as the various divergences offered span a wide expanse of tone, speed, coloration and impetus. This track is definitely the finest moment here, as it encapsulates those melodic elements found in their previous album. Perhaps the mercurial French band One Shot would be the closest in terms of stylistics but only barely. Their athletic and muscular form of jazzy prog sets them apart, in partnership with experimental forays that also benefit from occasional winks at the past legends. Originality, inspiration and impeccable delivery will keep the aether nice and clean for many years to come. 4.5 Sforza atmospheres

items.body: Review by Archisorcerus — The time-honoured Finns, i.e. Amorphis are one of the most prolific and prominent metal bands; and their name, beyond a shadow of a doubt, is already inscribed with golden letters on the magickal pages of the grand metal grimoire. But, are they prog? Well, I wouldn't say so... However, now that they are included in the archives here, they'll not be shunned by me by any means. In fact, for this album, contrariwise I'm gonna embrace them with my utmost sentimentality. This one is really one of my ultimate favourite albums, and it induces such indescribable sensations within my soul... Hence, I see no harm in giving this album 5 stars. I'm a bit surprised that it has received quite high ratings here, whilst it's also a nice surprise.So, why the surprise? Because Tuonela is an album that divided down the fans from around the middle. I first listened to it in the year it was out (1999), and I must say that I immediately fell in love. That was the time I got into university, and it evokes so many memories in me also from that beautiful period of my life. It is not just an ordinary album that I associate with a certain phase of my life, though; Tuonela still affects me profoundly after decades. As far as my view is concerned, Its soulfulness should always be reckoned with, even if its nostalgic value is abstracted. All in all, this is a timeless classic for me. I know that I'm far from being the sole super-admirer of the album, but lots of Amorphis fans were frustrated by this album, which is also understandable. Relativity... And also the band really changed their style with Tuonela, which I can say was even quite risky for their career.Aside from its emotional aspect, Tuonela has also some real alternative rock/metal vibes, which sets it apart from their previous/traditional albums. With Pasi Koskinen on vocals, they even went further in such experiments in their later albums, and eventually their adventure with Pasi ended. As I recollect, Koskinen said that he had lost his motivation for Amorphis and left the band. And then their era with Tomi Joutsen on vocals commenced... But, this issue belongs to another topic/review. Back on topic, Tuonela is a really deeply emotional album, and it has an unmatched manner of fusion to induce both melancholic and riveting feelings in listeners like me. For instance, Sakari Kukko really adds an enthralling charm with his flute and sax in the album, which in turn can make you feel rueful or rapturous. For another example, Pasi Koskinen's vocals can also arouse contrasting emotions respective to the songs/parts.Hard to pick a favourite or favourites from the album, and it really flows well throughout. Only the song entitled "Greed" punches up with its "brootal" vocals. Haha. I view this particular track as the weakest link in the album, howbeit perhaps it is not a link at all, but rather functions as a curiosity in an otherwise perfectly flowing album. It by no means urges me to make frantic splashes within the water, though. Perhaps if this album were "Silent Waters" that came out in the Joutsen era, things would be different... Anyways, Tuonela is as it should be, and perfect as it is Besides, a "villain" can surely add a rather thrilling aspect in such works. The greedy bastards can be anywhere, and some of them can be amusingly intriguing, you know... Ha-Ha!

items.body: Review by A Crimson Mellotron — 'Grimspound' is the tenth studio album from esteemed progressive rock band Big Big Train. There issomething really elegant and refined about this 2017 release, which represents what many refer to asa "middle period" for BBT. Dedicated to an exploration of progressive folk and pastoral soundscapes,albums like this one focus extensively on texture and composition, with the band combiningflawlessly acoustic elements with traditional rock and folk instrumentation. For me 'Grimspound' hasalways been some kind of an otherworldly release from the Bournemouth-based band, most likelybecause of the melodic approach to the songwriting on this record or the heavily symphonicundertones.Whatever it is, this album is the one that balances perfectly the band's retro prog leanings withtheir zealous taste for English folklore. Some of the writing on this record is exceptional, andthis is particularly true for tracks like 'Brave Captain', which is a wonderfully pastoral progsuite, the top-notch instrumental 'On the Racing Line', the beautiful title track, and the 15-minute-long epic 'A Mead Hall In Winter' that appears towards the end. The rest of the material onhere is really solid, and definitely impresses with a balanced, acute sound that tries to be pitch-perfect a little too much. Yet 'Grimspound' is not a perfect album, and songs like 'As The CrowFlies' and 'The Ivy Gate' do contain some soporific sections. 'Experimental Gentlemen' is excitingand develops rather interestingly, but its imposing length might not sit well with all listeners.All in all, 'Grimspound' has this rootsy atmosphere to it, and while it might be a difficult recordto get into at first, it becomes incredibly pleasing with careful, repeated listens.

items.body: Review by vmagistr — My favorite music historian and music encyclopedist, Piero Scaruffi, puts forward the thesis that blues initially had the dominant influence on rock as a genre, with jazz subsequently taking over that role. He considers 1967 to be the imaginary dividing line at which the scales of influence tipped irreversibly. Like any theory, this one isn't entirely applicable, but the idea that the jazz concept of "melodic theme?instrumental solo passages?melodic theme" lives on in rock guitar and keyboard solos ? and possibly also in those bass and drum ones ? strikes me as interesting and compelling.Jazz influences alone cannot fully explain the work of early King Crimson, whose origins were a loose evolution of the eclectic psychedelia of the trio Giles, Giles and Fripp (guitarist Robert Fripp, for example, had a lifelong fondness for classical music and big band music), but they are evident in their music like few other elements. On the debut album In the Court of the Crimson King, this is true, for example, of the opening whirlwind 21st Century Schizoid Man, in which the band interspersed perfectly rehearsed instrumental passages with moments of near-cacophony. They went even further (and, for my taste, too far) in the improvisational exercise that unfolds from the brief ballad Moonchild. Ten minutes of those "plinks, clacks, clicks, and clangs" tend to be too much for my patience, which is why I skip them without hesitation when listening.The tracks I Talk to the Wind and Epitaph build their atmosphere in a distinctly different direction. I enjoy their ballad-like feel with a touch of pathos (especially in the latter), the inventive chord progressions, and "something" borrowed from classical music. Ian McDonald wasn�t by any means the first to use wind instruments and the mellotron in rock music, but he added sonic colors and textures that were unique for their time. In the title track, most of what I've mentioned above comes together in a majestic, though at times somewhat ponderous hymn. It's an enthralling piece, but I probably wouldn't mind if the finale were, say, a third shorter ? the extended ending just sounds to me like an attempt to make full use of the space on the vinyl LP.The unifying theme of the album's lyrics is obvious ? disillusion in all its forms. Through expressive imagery of napalm hell and post-traumatic stress disorder (21st Century Schizoid Man), fears of nuclear war (Epitaph), and the Crowleyan struggle between good and evil (Moonchild), a common thread of an unpleasant premonition runs through it all: we, mankind, have lost, and that we'd be better off not even thinking too much about any future. At times, this makes the narrator thoroughly pissed off at the rulers of this world (The Court of the Crimson King); at other times, he doesn't hesitate to speak his mind to God himself (I Talk to the Wind). The summer of love is over; the depression of the 1970s is on the horizon.I consider the album In the Court of the Crimson King to be a compelling piece of music. While I can't quite take it in as a whole, I find enough good (even excellent) elements on it to make me return to it often and with pleasure. In my opinion, it was more significant for the burgeoning art rock scene than any other album from that year, but in King Crimson's discography, it remains just below the top for me.

items.body: Review by tszirmay — Still going strong after all these years, especially in lieu of the fact that the preceding release was a smash by all accounts , as 'In Spiral' (2022) was quite inspired and spirited, to say the least. Jean-Pascal Boffo is a veteran multi-instrumentalist , though it's his guitar skills that have stood the test of time, and this new one marks 40 years of a rather stellar career. Ably abetted by drummers Wiliam Bur and Franck Agulhon, synth player S'raphin Palmeri , saxophonist Pierre Coq Amann and Thomas Seignert handling bass duties. ' Inner World' owns a striking cover, expressing the need for introspection in an increasing manic world laden with data overkill/fatigue. Perhaps a willing passage into one's childhood may be the ultimate refuge. We shall certainly find out where the music will take us, through a dozen lush tracks. The introspective voyage begins with the intricately nebulous 'Neverwhere' , a yearningly romantic groove into an ethereal world where Boffo's electric guitars dare to wander, combining slick riffs and splashy chords with sensual slivers of melodic lines, leaving the saxophone to further the seduction. The sparse finale is astonishing. 'Desert Life' keeps the arid dunes aglow with sandy reminiscences, as if a caravanserai of purity was crossing the Sahara, in search of the little prince. The swirling sax casts the necessary spell, entrancing and mystifying as it fades into the sweltering horizon. Taking the hypnotic sentiment even further, albeit in a more modern approach, not far removed from 'Impossible Guitars'-era Phil Manzanera, 'Mantra' coils magically like an obedient cobra, the saxophone again taking the spotlight, with superb rhythmic support from Seignert and the drum kit. Underneath the swirl, the fretboard exercises immense creative euphoria , without being overtly splashy, a true sign of class. The trio of tracks all have this unique soft outro that is most immediately noticeable. The drum work gets intricate on 'Anything Can Happen Here', pushed along by athletic guitar cycles that recall his previous use of a technique made famous by Robert Fripp and Andy Summers among others, while 'From the Moon to the Earth' patrols more cosmic expanses, ambient floating obelisks of sound that gleam in the dark void, at times somber reminders that lifeless orbiting satellites can be devoid of anything but endless memories. The obscure ambience of 'Parallel World' proves the point that opposites can nevertheless remain very close, often just a threshold to cross over into the proverbial other side. A tremendous example of sonic restraint, where less is more, and still utterly convincing. Boffo displays these traits with a light touch that is applause worthy. There may be peace to be found in the end, in some concealed Shangri-La within one's soul. Speaking of Everest, 'Elevation' cannot get any higher on our planet, and here, the focus is on a cinematic exploration of the inner self, thinking freely in rarified air, devoid of any spiritual pollution, pondering the truth on 'The Expanse' as it lays serenely below us, amid the clouds.As if tele-transported to an opposite realm where mechanical thought reigns supreme, 'Robotown' is an electronic fantasy that speaks volumes of where humanity now stands, a world where send/receive, edit/delete and like/follow rule our agenda-heavy time. The concrete sequencer arrangement is led by muscular tik-tok percussion, and occasional wafts of oblique guitar shards that provide some semblance of humanity. This comes shining through on the more luxuriant 'Ubiquity' where Boffo's organic axe gets to surf atop the synthesized bubble bath platform created by Palmeri's arsenal. To quote some pointy-eared Vulcan mister, 'Fascinating!'.A penultimate longer track clocking in at 6 minutes and change, 'A Dream within a Dream' perfectly encapsulates the essence of this album's concept, as it liberates the artist to express his innermost feelings, without any constraint forced upon him. The fluid guitar lines unite with the expressive sax urges, all rhythmically ensconced in a light passageway that soothes the soul, the melodies beyond attractive, perhaps even meditative. The rather gorgeous 'Farewell' is a scary closing title, as it may infer a sense of finality, which would be a disappointment. Boffo can and should definitely continue on the path chosen with 'In Spiral', as his last two albums are the cream of his crop, in my humblest of opinions. A level of maturity that bodes well for the future. A bientot !4.5 innermost sanctums

items.body: Review by A Crimson Mellotron — 'Quantum Gate' is a major studio album from Tangerine Dream, originally issued in 2017, andrepresenting the group's first studio release following founding member Edgar Froese's passing inearly 2015. Under the direction of Thorsten Quaeschning, 'Quantum Gate' stands as the firstinstallment in TD's Quantum Years, which is ultimately a new phase that has the aim of providing acontemporary spin to the trademark sound of the German progressive electronic group, while exploringa range of sequencer-driven tones, non-musical ideas and various outside influences. Joined byviolinist Hoshiko Yamane and synth player Ulrich Schnauss, Quaeschning and his fellows carefullyconstructed this tremendous album from sketches and concepts prepared by Froese himself, whileworking out the new musical direction of his project. The final product undoubtedly matches theambition and vision of Froese, and the spacey synthwave sound of 'Quantum Gate' is inherentlymodern, eclectic and a tad bit nostalgic.And thus, we have a really impressive collection of various Tangerine Dream compositions, withatmospheric opener 'Sensing Elements' setting a somewhat futuristic tone that impresses with a vividpalette of shimmering synth sequences. The thirteen minutes of this track allow the trio to unleasha range of sounds that rivals the progressive nature and musical ambition of Tangerine Dream's earlyclassic works. This is followed by 'Roll the Seven Twice', a six-minute-long piece that offers anelemental sound and introduces some EDM influences, while third track 'Granular Blankets' prescribesa spacey atmosphere that feels a little darker than usual. The upbeat tempo of the next two tracksis rather enjoyable and perhaps surprising, and for me, this is the part of the album that reallyfeels very contemporary. 'Non-Locality Destination' is another monolithic collage of electronicsounds, taking up some ten minutes' worth of music, followed by two more beautifully futuristiccompositions. The closing track 'Genesis of Precious Thoughts' concludes the album with arhythmically stimulating sound that looks back towards Tangerine Dream's progressive-orientedmusical origins.'Quantum Gate' is one of the strongest and most inspired albums by TD in many years - a record thatreminisces the haunting atmosphere of the group's classic releases, while offering an excitingmodern spin to their trademark sound.

items.body: Review by UMUR — "Symphonique" is a live album release by Canadian thrash/progressive metal act Voivod. The album wasreleased through Century Media Records in June 2026. As the title suggests it�s a live album withVoivod playing with an classical orchestra. The album was recorded live on 4th of June 2025 at theGrand Th��tre in Qu�bec City, Canada with the Quebec Symphony Orchestra. Most of the material on the12 tracks, 72:44 minutes long album is culled from Voivod�s 1987-1991 period but there are a coupleof newer tracks and one older one ("Nuclear War") on the track list too.Combining the live performance of a rock/metal act with a classical orchestra is not a new thing andloads of other rock/metal acts have done this prior to Voivod doing it on "Symphonique". DeepPurple, Procol Harum, and Metallica are just some of the artists who have done it. Attempts by thementioned artists and other artists who has done it have been of varying quality and often it hasresulted in live recordings which sound like the rock/metal band playing their parts and theclassical orchestra playing their parts with little connection between them.While there are moments on "Symphonique" where the rock/metal band and classical orchestra parts geland come together nicely, unfortunately there are plenty of sections where they don�t. I�m sure itwas a fun experiment for Voivod and if I got the chance with my band I�d probably take it too, butthe rawness and intensity of Voivod�s material is often overpowered by the might of the classicalorchestra and some unsuitable arrangements. I felt the same when I listened to Metallica�s "S&M"(1999) live with a classical orchestra album. The band and the classical orchestra simply too oftensound like they are on separate stages recording their parts. It�s often during intros or specificsections during songs where the classical orchestra parts work, but since they are omnipresent andthere is a full score for each track, it�s all a bit bombastic and lacking dynamics.The sound production values are not top notch either. The band sound weak in the soundscape andSnake sounds a bit rusty. All harsh words...I know. But I had great hopes for this release and"Symphonique" unfortunately delivers everything I had feared it would instead of delivering what Ihad hoped. It�s another rock/metal band meets classical orchestra waisted opportunity. Despite myrelatively obvious negativity towards "Symphonique", it�s not a terrible release and I�m sure thereare some who would find it interesting and therefore a 3 star (60%) rating isn�t all wrong, althoughmy personal rating is maybe a bit lower.(Originally posted on Metal Music Archives).

items.body: “Color Paraná” is named after one image: the ochre, deep colour of the Paraná river that runs past Rosario in Argentina, carried in the eyes of a lover left on the far side of the ocean. It’s the new single from Luazó, the project of French guitarist and composer Robin Gentien, and a love song that moves between Paris, Rosario and San Basilio de Palenque, the Afro-Colombian town near Cartagena. Luazó started as his goodbye to Latin America: Gentien cut the first EP in Buenos Aires the week before he left the continent, after years on the move, and the project came out of playing with Colombian drummer Pablo Cruz. It’s part Latin jazz, part what he calls desert cumbia, a slow and slightly cheeky groove, with a guitar that owes as much to Tinariwen and Ali Farka Touré as to Santana. The song carries the ache of distance and a breakup, and underneath it the wish to come back and start again. Out via the Paris label Panache and recorded at the city’s Studio Hippocampus, “Color Paraná” folds a decade of Gentien’s travelling between Europe and the Americas into one warm, unhurried cumbia. items.body: Giuseppe Verticchio already has a rich discography to his name, and earlier this year he added another remarkable work to it. The album consists of 14 tracks, all of which—except for the closing piece—previously appeared on various compilations released between 2017 and 2025. It has been described as perhaps his darkest work to date: a tunnel with no light at the end, reflecting the vision of a world that grows more decadent with each passing day. The selection of tracks is undeniably dark, but not exclusively so. A considerable degree of diversity can be found throughout the album, which is hardly surprising given that the material spans several years of creative output. Nimh moves effortlessly between pure Ambient, dark Ballad-like compositions, Cinematic soundscapes, and Experimental passages. The opening track even features harsh vocals. Giuseppe Verticchio remains closely connected to his guitar, coaxing from it sounds of pure melancholy while also creating dreamy atmospheres that perfectly complement the album’s Cinematic character. At the same time, a variety of noises, textures, and subtle sonic manipulations enrich the background. The final track, a previously unreleased composition, fits seamlessly within the album’s dimension. One moment, Nimh makes us drift weightlessly; the next, it leaves us unsettled and trembling. Giuseppe Verticchio is clearly far from finished and continues to surprise and captivate listeners with his unique musical vision and immersive sonic experiences. (Rating:7½). Listen to “Succumbing To The New Conquistadores”: https://nimh-music.bandcamp.com/track/succumbing-to-the-new-conquistadores

items.body: Belgian EBM act Front 242 have released “Black Out” via Alfa Matrix. The live album was recorded at AB Brussels (Ancienne Belgique) in January 2025 and documents the band’s farewell run, with more than 40 performances across six months in Europe and the US. For “Black Out,” Patrick Codenys, Jean-Luc De Meyer, and Richard23 are joined on stage by Tim Kroker, while David Baboulis of Soldout handled the studio mixing and production. Black Out (Deluxe Edition + 3 Hidden Bonus Tracks) by FRONT 242 Across Bandcamp and the Alfa Matrix store, “Black Out” is available as a digital edition, a 23-track 2CD digipak, a crystal clear 2LP. The 2CD adds three exclusive tracks: “MasterHit,” “Soul Manager,” and “No Shuffle.” The release came also out as a totally sold out limited clear purple 2LP fanpack, a totally sold out Core Selected Pack, and a totally sold out Total Access Pack. The limited purple-vinyl fanpack includes a tote bag, armband, 20x30cm art print, two glass coasters, and the label compilations “Sounds From The Matrix 026 & 027,” this edition was limited to 1,000 copies worldwide and sold out in just a few days. The Core Selected Pack combines the 2CD, the purple-vinyl fanpack, and the 2CD tribute “Recovery 2 For You,” while the Total Access Pack adds the crystal clear 2LP to that bundle. A new fan pack for “Black Out” was made available as well. This updated ‘Essential Pack‘ includes the crystal clear double vinyl along with a selection of additional items and is still available. Black Out (incl. 3 bonus tracks) 2CD Black Out (incl. 3 bonus tracks) download Black Out (Core Selected Pack) SOLD OUT Black Out (Total Access Pack) SOLD OUT Black Out 2LP (limited fanpack edition clear purple vinyl) SOLD OUT Black Out 2LP (crystal clear vinyl) Black Out (Essential Pack) Note that the special packs also include the new “Recovery 2 For You (Tribute to Front 242)” 2CD. About Front 242 Front 242 started in Aarschot, Belgium in 1981. Daniel Bressanutti and Dirk Bergen launched the project first. Patrick Codenys and Jean-Luc De Meyer joined in time for “Geography” in 1982, and Richard Jonckheere, better known as Richard 23, followed in 1983. The band’s first single was “Body to Body” in 1981. By 1984 Front 242 had signed to Wax Trax! in Chicago, and “Take One” became their first U.S. release. “No Comment” followed in 1984, “Official Version” in 1987 and “Front by Front” in 1988. Front 242 continued with “Tyranny >For You<” in 1991, then “06:21:03:11 Up Evil” and “05:22:09:12 Off” in 1993. A hiatus followed, before the four core members reunited in 1997 with Tim Kroker on drums for the live setup. “Pulse” arrived in 2003. Alfa Matrix, which had in the meantime release the band’s side-projects then started to release anniversary editions and vinyl reissues. The band’s live career ended with the “Black Out” farewell run with the gig on January 25, 2025 at Ancienne Belgique in Brussels being the band’s final show.

items.body: Idoru and Back From The Wave have released “Love Is Not Enough“, a debut collaboration issued on Iptamenos Discos, the Berlin-based label run by Local Suicide. The EBM and electroclash track came out on June 10, 2026 as a digital single. It pairs the Miami-based dark electronic artist Idoru with the French producer Back From The Wave. “Love Is Not Enough” began as a cross-continental exchange of ideas between the two artists and grew into a club track built on a raw EBM drive, a distorted electroclash bassline and Idoru’s vocals. The lyrics deal with the aftermath of a relationship built on illusion. The single is available to stream and download. Love Is Not Enough (ISI012) by Idoru & Back From The Wave Iptamenos Discos, founded by the Berlin duo Local Suicide, has previously released music from Kalipo, Dina Summer, Skelesys and Curses. About Idoru and Back From The Wave Idoru is a Detroit-born, Miami-based artist who works in dark electronic music, mixing minimal techno, industrial, electro and Italo. She is a founder of the Manta Recordings label and releases through her own Bandcamp page. Earlier releases include the singles “Take My Hand”, which carried a Damon Jee remix, and “Like A Machine”. In 2025 she joined the German darkwave act SIIE on the single “Violent”, which featured remixes from Panther Modern and Skelesys. “Love Is Not Enough” is her first collaboration with Back From The Wave. Back From The Wave is the project of the French producer Fred, who blends electro, techno, Italo and EBM. He began releasing electronic music in the early 2000s on the French labels Goodlife and Scandium, and his later work has appeared on labels including Ritmo Fatale, Space Factory and Bordello A Parigi. The 2025 release “Escape From The Void” came out through Factor City. With “Love Is Not Enough”, Back From The Wave makes his debut on Iptamenos Discos alongside Idoru.

items.body: execunit‘s “Humanicide” is the new two-track single from the Swedish electronic project that blends industrial synthpop with krautrock-inspired electronics. The single is out now through Town And Towers Records and is available across streaming services. The project is the work of Andreas Rimheden, who writes, performs and produces the music without the use of AI. The project takes its cues from the robotic music of Kraftwerk, the soundtrack work of John Carpenter, and early industrial and German krautrock, aiming for a sound built around electronics and rusted metal. The single is available to stream and download across major platforms. “Humanicide” follows execunit’s debut single “Rust”, which Side-Line covered in Execunit returns with ‘Rust’ single in March 2024, also released through Town And Towers Records. The project’s debut album “Prophecy” is on streaming services, and Town And Towers Records opens CD pre-orders for the new album on 8 July 2026. About execunit execunit is a Swedish electronic act based in Malmö and is the project of Andreas Rimheden, who also records as Eternity Range and was a member of the 1990s Swedish dark electronic group Morticians. Rimheden initialized execunit in 2022 to realize a long-held idea: a project that sounds as if it were made by machines, for machines, with a machine-like priest or prophet as its only voice. The project signed to the Danish label Town And Towers Records and issued its first single, “Rust”, on 15 March 2024. Its lead vocals are mechanical and artificial, narrating a coming singularity in which machines become sentient and turn against their creators. The two-track single “Humanicide” continues that narrative and marks execunit’s move toward a darker, more club-focused sound ahead of the CD edition of the debut album “Prophecy”.

items.body: Glass Eden, the Hannover darkwave project of Sarah Egger, released the debut album “Born From A Wish” on June 17, 2026. Egger wrote, recorded, and produced the eight-track record at home, and issued it digitally through the project’s Bandcamp page. It is the first release under the Glass Eden name, which Egger started in 2025 after years in other bands. She built the songs alone, around analog synthesizers and English-language lyrics. The solo method became the point of the record as much as its method. Egger says this: “To create a musical universe totally on my own felt empowering and like therapy during a year that was emotional and challenging.” The arrangements rest on three synthesizers: a Korg Polysix, a Behringer Pro-800, and a Yamaha DX7. Across its eight tracks, the album moves between minimal synth, coldwave, and dreampop, using drum-machine rhythms and English-language vocals. “Born From A Wish” runs eight tracks: “No Place”, “Between The Lines”, “Sleepless”, “No Time”, “This Night”, “Therapy”, “Leave This Place”, and “Not free”. Australian producer and mastering engineer Morgan Wright mixed and mastered the album. Daniel Egger plays guitar on “This Night”, and Nicolas Marquardt contributes the modular-synth sample on “Between The Lines”. Born From A Wish by Glass Eden A video accompanies “Leave This Place”. The album is available digitally; listeners can order “Born From A Wish” on Bandcamp, and the record also streams on Spotify. About Glass Eden Sarah Egger is a musician based in Hannover, Germany. Her route to Glass Eden ran through two earlier projects. In 2012 she founded the synthpop duo The Colder Sea with Daniel Egger, releasing music through the French label Synth Religion. She later worked on the project COLD CALL. with Nicolas Marquardt and Daniel Egger, which moved her writing toward coldwave and darkwave. Egger started Glass Eden in 2025 and produced on her own for the first time. The result, “Born From A Wish”, arrived on June 17, 2026 as the project’s debut album, self-produced at home and mixed and mastered by Morgan Wright. It is Glass Eden’s first record and Egger’s first as a solo producer.

items.body: Damage, the synth-punk band formed in Orlando, Florida and now based in Brooklyn, New York, have released the “How To Talk To Humans” remix EP, a digital set that reworks the title track and adds two new originals. The remix EP follows the “How To Talk To Humans” EP that the band issued on May 15, 2026 through their own Space Fish Records, in a run that covered 12″ vinyl, CD and streaming. Two new Damage originals include “Carriage Horses”, a harder track, and “How To Talk To Humans” which gives the EP its title. Around them sit a series of remixes built from source tracks produced by Joe Livingston and the band. The remixers are New York’s Richie Dio, Providence’s Knowlton Walsh, Tommy “MOT” Barger, who contributes a “Dance Don’t Dance” remix, and Livingston himself. Damage says that the EP is a step outside its usual hardcore mode. The band add that the EP is “a unique experiment in the history of Damage, bringing together a series of remixes based on source tracks produced by Joe Livingston and the band.” How To Talk To Humans – Remix EP by Damage The remix EP is available to stream and download through the band’s Bandcamp page. The “How To Talk To Humans” EP is available on 12″ vinyl and CD from Space Fish Records, alongside streaming. The band has also shared an official video for the title track, “How To Talk To Humans“. About Damage Damage formed in Orlando, Florida in the early 1980s. The group began as Brain Damage and shortened the name for an early gig. From the start the band built its sound on live drums and analog synthesizers, with no guitars, an approach shared with bands like The Screamers, Suicide and Units. Mike Brown led the project on vocals and synthesizer, playing a Moog Liberation keytar that he has kept on stage across the band’s run. Early releases included the 1984 “Polar Bears” 7″ EP and the 1986 “Synthology” album. The band founded Space Fish Records and ran the Club Space Fish venue in Orlando, which closed after a GG Allin performance on November 18, 1991. Through the 1980s and early 1990s Damage shared stages with Adolescents, Dead Kennedys, Adrenaline O.D., Battalion of Saints, SNFU, Fugazi, The Flaming Lips and Alien Sex Fiend. After a hiatus of roughly 35 years, Damage returned to recording and performing in 2024 and released “Modern World”, their fourth studio album, on Space Fish Records in 2025. The current lineup pairs founding member Mike Brown (vocals, synthesizer) with Joe Livingston (drums) and Joshua Clark (synthesizer, backing vocals). The “How To Talk To Humans” remix EP is out as download, vinyl and CD.
